intro: Google Sheets for research librarians on Mac is a powerful way to organize large datasets and track systematic review progress. While it runs in your browser, using Google Sheets on a Mac allows you to integrate your spreadsheet data with your other research tools like Zotero or Obsidian.

blocks.text: Setting up your Google Sheets environment on Mac

Google Sheets does not have a native Mac app. It lives in your browser. For a better experience, use Google Chrome. You can create a dedicated window to keep your research sheets separate from your daily browsing. Open sheets.google.com in Chrome. Click the three-dot menu in the top right corner. Select Save and Share. Then click Install page as app. This puts a shortcut in your Applications folder and Launchpad.

You likely handle large datasets for systematic reviews. The most common issues involve broken formulas and permission errors. If you see a #REF! error, it means you deleted a row or column that a formula relied on. Always check your ranges before deleting data. If you have multiple Google accounts, you might hit permission errors. Use a dedicated Chrome profile for your library work to avoid account conflicts.

Speed matters when you have hundreds of rows to clean. Press ⌘ + / to see the full list of shortcuts. Use ⌘ + ⇧ + H to find and replace text in your search logs. If you need to hide rows while scanning data, use ⌘ + ⌥ + 9. To hide columns, use ⌘ + ⌥ + 0. These small actions save minutes every hour.

items: Use [Filter views](/how-to/add-a-filter-to-a-range-in-google-sheets) to sort data without changing the view for colleagues.
Keep your search strings clean by using [Split text into columns](/how-to/split-text-into-columns-in-google-sheets) when importing raw data.
[Remove duplicate rows](/how-to/remove-duplicate-rows-in-google-sheets) immediately after importing citations from Zotero or other databases.
Use [Freeze columns](/how-to/freeze-columns-in-google-sheets) to keep your citation titles visible while you scroll through metadata.

blocks.text: What to do when formulas fail

Formula errors are frustrating. The #NAME? error often happens if you mistype a function name. Check for extra spaces or missing commas. If you are counting unique values, use the UNIQUE function combined with COUNTIF. Always test your formulas on a small sample of data before applying them to your entire sheet.

Librarians often share spreadsheets with faculty. Use [View only access](/how-to/share-with-view-only-access-in-google-sheets) when you want to provide data without risking accidental edits. If you need to track changes, use the [Revision history](/how-to/see-revision-history-in-google-sheets) feature. It shows exactly who changed what and when.

faq.question: Is there a real Google Sheets app for Mac?
faq.answer: No, there is no official native app. You can create a web shortcut in Chrome to make it act like one.

faq.question: How do I fix #REF! errors?
faq.answer: These errors occur when a cell reference is broken. Check your formulas to ensure they point to valid cells and ranges.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur to help with my spreadsheets?
